quote: Not all apps need Redux. It's important to understand the kind of application you're building... Dan Abramov, one of the creators of Redux, says: 'I would like to amend this: don't use Redux until you have problems with vanilla React.'

quote: npm trends comparison of @reduxjs/toolkit vs jotai vs mobx vs recoil vs redux vs zustand download counts over time.

claim: The State of React 2025 survey reports Zustand gaining ground fast on Redux and leading on user satisfaction.
quote: Redux and its successor Redux Toolkit have long been the most widespread state management solutions, but Zustand is gaining ground fast.

claim: State of React usage trend 2023-2025: Redux 80.5%->75.5%, Redux Toolkit flat ~54%, Zustand 28%->50%, Jotai 13%->19%; bundle sizes Zustand ~1.2KB vs RTK ~12KB gzip.
quote: Redux (plain): 2023: 80.5% -> 2025: 75.5% (declining). Redux Toolkit: Remained flat at approximately 54%. Zustand: 2023: 28% -> 2025: 50%. Jotai: 2023: 13% -> 2025: 19%.

Redux Toolkit's contributor graph is dominated by Mark Erikson (1437 commits), with aryaemami59 (924), EskiMojo14 (447), phryneas (346) - a small core team and a real bus-factor concentration.

claim: Redux Toolkit's stated purpose is to fix three complaints: store config too complicated, too many packages needed, too much boilerplate.
quote: Redux Toolkit addresses three common concerns: 'Configuring a Redux store is too complicated', 'I have to add a lot of packages to get Redux to do anything useful', 'Redux requires too much boilerplate code'.

claim: The Redux maintainers state that anyone writing Redux logic today should be using Redux Toolkit.
quote: If you are writing _any_ Redux logic today, you _should_ be using Redux Toolkit to write that code!

claim: The official RTK Query comparison page positions RTK Query as the choice when you already use Redux, and admits it deliberately does not normalize/deduplicate cached items the way alternatives can.
quote: RTK Query deliberately does _not_ implement a cache that would deduplicate identical items across multiple requests. ... We think that all of those tools are great!

claim: React 19 shipped Actions, useActionState, useOptimistic and use(), covering pending state, error handling and optimistic rollback natively; Server Components require a supporting framework/bundler.
quote: Actions provide a pending state that starts at the beginning of a request and automatically resets when the final state update is committed... Actions support the new useOptimistic hook so you can show users instant feedback while the requests are submitting... Actions provide error handling so you can display Error Boundaries when a request fails, and revert optimistic updates to their original value automatically.

claim: useOptimistic renders an optimistic state immediately during an async action and automatically reverts on failure - the pattern that used to require Redux middleware.
quote: useOptimistic is a React Hook that lets you optimistically update the UI.

claim: Zustand's devtools middleware connects to the Redux DevTools Extension and gives action logging and time-travel debugging without Redux.
quote: The devtools middleware lets you use Redux DevTools Extension without Redux and enables time-travel debugging of your store.

claim: Redux's own testing guide recommends integration tests over unit-testing reducers and selectors, and calls Redux code an implementation detail.
quote: Prefer writing integration tests with everything working together... In the majority of scenarios, the end-user does not know, and does not care whether Redux is used within the application at all. As such, the Redux code can be treated as an implementation detail of the app, without requiring explicit tests for the Redux code in many circumstances.

claim: Redux's derived-state story is memoized selectors via Reselect's createSelector, keeping stored state minimal and computing the rest.
quote: We specifically recommend that Redux apps should keep the Redux state minimal, and derive additional values from that state as needed. ... memoized selectors... using libraries like Reselect.

claim: Reselect is the standard memoized-selector library for Redux derived state.
quote: Selector library for Redux

claim: redux-undo provides undo/redo and action history for reducers by wrapping them - the action log is the substrate that makes undo/redo cheap in Redux.
quote: simple undo/redo functionality for redux state containers

claim: RTK Query ships a first-party OpenAPI code generator, @rtk-query/codegen-openapi, that produces a fully typed API slice with hooks from a Swagger/OpenAPI schema.
quote: RTK Query's API and architecture is oriented around declaring API endpoints up front. This lends itself well to automatically generating API slice definitions from external API schema definitions, such as OpenAPI and GraphQL.

claim: Orval generates typed TanStack Query hooks (plus MSW mocks) from an OpenAPI schema - the non-Redux equivalent of RTK Query's codegen.
quote: orval is able to generate client with appropriate type-signatures (TypeScript) from any valid OpenAPI v3 or Swagger v2 specification, either in yaml or json formats.

claim: Hey API is the current frontrunner for OpenAPI-to-TypeScript generation and has a TanStack Query plugin.
quote: Turn your OpenAPI specification into a beautiful TypeScript client

claim: Zustand is a minimal hook-based store with no provider, no reducers and no action types.
quote: Bear necessities for state management in React

claim: TanStack Query is the dominant server-state/caching library, actively maintained.
quote: Powerful asynchronous state management, server-state utilities and data fetching for the web.

claim: Redux ships an official Style Guide of enforced conventions - the mechanism by which large teams get uniformity.
quote: This is the official style guide for writing Redux code. It lists our recommended patterns, best practices, and suggested approaches for writing Redux applications.

claim: Practitioner comparison: TanStack Query replaces the server-state portion of Redux, which is 60-80% of Redux code in data-driven apps; new projects increasingly start with TanStack Query alone and add a store only when client-state complexity demands it.
quote: TanStack Query replaces the portion of Redux that was handling server state synchronization - often 60-80% of Redux code in data-driven applications.

claim: Redux DevTools provides time-travel debugging by stepping through the action history; it is a separate repo consumed by both Redux and Zustand.
quote: DevTools for Redux with hot reloading, action replay, and customizable UI

claim: RTK Query's 2.x/3.x roadmap is an open discussion thread driven by the maintainer; RTKQ work was intentionally deferred until after RTK 2.0 shipped.
quote: RTK Query 2.x / 3.x roadmap planning

claim: Community sentiment in 2026: Redux is not dead but should not be a default; much of the problem it solved was absorbed by the ecosystem around it.
quote: Redux isn't dead, but in 2026, maybe we shouldn't be using it without thinking, like opening jQuery to create a dropdown.

claim: Jotai is the atomic-state alternative, a real but smaller niche.
quote: Primitive and flexible state management for React

claim: TanStack Query's own docs frame it as a server-state manager that replaces the boilerplate of caching/fetching but not a general client-state store.
quote: TanStack Query is a server-state library, responsible for managing asynchronous operations between your server and client. ... TanStack Query is not a replacement for local/client state management. ... you may find that most of your once seemingly global state really wasn't global at all.

claim: Redux's official positioning: a predictable state container answering 'when did a certain slice of state change, and where did the data come from'.
quote: Redux is a pattern and library for managing and updating global application state, where the UI triggers events called 'actions' to describe what happened.
